ny_peterskill.blurb: Peterskill is a one-pitch cliff band within Minnewaska State Park Preserve, in the Gunks area of New York. The rock is quartzite conglomerate, so expect roofs, horizontal cracks and gear-protected lines that are just one rope length high. Traditional routes make up most of the climbing, backed by a healthy group of top-rope lines and a busy bouldering zone, with problems from V0 up to roughly V7. Roped grades run from easy up into the 5.12s and 5.13, though most sit between 5.8 and 5.11. Dickie Barre, the newer upper cliff, offers cracks, grooves, steep harder lines and big capping roofs. The short walls suit climbers learning to lead or build anchors.

nc_moore_s_wall_bouldering.blurb: This is the boulder side of Moore's Wall in Hanging Rock State Park, out in the Piedmont of North Carolina not far from Winston-Salem. The stone is quartzite, and the problems are spread over several separate boulderfields rather than one big talus slope. Sentinel Buttress holds the largest share, followed by the Valley Boulderfield, Two Mile and the North End, with Two Mile sitting at the end of a longer walk than the rest. Difficulty leans toward intermediate and advanced, with the bulk between V2 and V6, a good number of V0 and V1 warm-ups, and a tail of hard problems up to V10.

wi_west_bluff_north.blurb: West Bluff North covers the northern half of the hill above the western shore of Devil's Lake, in the Baraboo Range of Wisconsin. It is bouldering only, on quartzite talus scattered over a slope that faces east. Problems are split between a lower group reached from the trail along the base of the bluff and an upper group above it, plus a small wall near the Ice Age trailhead. Expect a broad spread from V0 to V9 and beyond, with the heart of the grades at V2 to V7 and a mix of slabs, highballs and overhanging lines. The talus is awkward to navigate, and some boulder fields are open and sunny while others sit in tree shade.

ar_lake_lincoln.blurb: Lake Lincoln is a small lakeside crag in the Ozarks west of Fayetteville in Northwest Arkansas. Bouldering is the biggest draw, spread over the Dam Boulders, Beauty School, Mad Max and several smaller clusters, with most problems between V0 and V6. Sport routes come next, mostly 5.8 to 5.11, along with a few trad lines. The walls are not tall, which makes it a friendly place for a first outdoor day, and the grade spread covers beginners through intermediates well. Harder climbers will find a handful of tougher lines but not a lot of them. Boulder approaches can be confusing at first, so allow time to find the problems.

ca_woodfords_canyon.blurb: Woodfords Canyon drops toward Nevada along the West Fork Carson River, on the east side of Carson Pass in Alpine County, a short drive from South Lake Tahoe. The granite is coarse and knobby, and the climbing is mostly traditional crack and corner work on crags about half a rope long, with a few sport lines, toprope options and a boulder zone. Most routes fall between 5.9 and 5.11, with a handful reaching 5.12 and 5.13. The Fortress, Cloudburst Canyon and Crystal Springs Canyon hold the most routes. Its two faces make it a year-round area: south-facing walls catch winter sun, while shaded north-facing walls take over in summer. Approaches over talus can be tiring, and crowds stay light.

id_fins_the.blurb: The Fins is a limestone sport-climbing area at the southern end of the Lost River Range in central Idaho, high up around 7,700 feet. Nearly everything here is bolted, on walls from vertical to a little overhanging, with edges, pockets and some sharp texture. Grades run from 5.10 to 5.13, with most routes between 5.10 and 5.12, so it suits strong moderate and hard climbers rather than beginners. Mortal Earth, the biggest sub-area, is newer and lower, with grey limestone and chert that gives plenty of holds, and it holds more moderate lines. Walls generally get morning sun and fall into shade by early afternoon, which keeps hot days climbable.
